explanations.explanation: David, whose psalm this is, says he's distraught "…at the voice of the enemy, at the pressure of the wicked." It's people doing this to him, not a bug going around. He says they bring down disaster on him and resent him in their anger. I think anybody who has had someone's voice rattle around their head all day gets that.

David never mentions being sick in this psalm. He says he's distraught "…at the voice of the enemy, at the pressure of the wicked." So the trouble is coming from people, not from his body. Nobody here is reaching for a thermometer and telling him to rest.

No famine shows up anywhere in these verses. David says he's distraught "…at the voice of the enemy, at the pressure of the wicked." The pressure is coming from people, and the psalm says they resent him in their anger. The empty shelves belong to a different book.
David says the opposite. He says, "My heart pounds within me, and the terrors of death assail me." That's a heart racing, not a heart on a hammock. He also says fear and trembling grip him.

Right, he's not calm at all. David says, "My heart pounds within me, and the terrors of death assail me." Then he adds that fear and trembling grip him and horror has overwhelmed him. He doesn't dress it up, and he says it straight to God.

David says, "Oh, that I had wings like a dove!" He's not asking for a bigger sword. He's asking for a way out, because he says he would fly away and find rest. I think when you're that worn down, rest sounds better than any fight.
Feet are close, since David does want to get away. But the psalm gives him wings, not hooves. He says, "Oh, that I had wings like a dove!" A dove can just lift off and leave the whole mess below it.
David isn't wishing to be tougher here. He's wishing to be gone. He says, "Oh, that I had wings like a dove!" and says he would fly away and find rest.
Rest is the word. David says that with wings like a dove he would "…fly away and find rest." He doesn't say he'd win anything or get anybody back. I think he's just tired all the way down.
Revenge never comes up in his wish. David says he would "…fly away and find rest." Nobody is on his list in that dream, he just wants out of the storm.
David isn't dreaming about money here. He says he would "…fly away and find rest." Wings, a quiet place, and a break from the noise is the whole wish.

David says, "In the wilderness I would remain." Not just a quick visit either, he says he would stay. Far from the noise is where he pictures rest. Then comes "Selah," and I'll let you sit with that picture a moment.
No palace in this dream. David says, "In the wilderness I would remain." He pictures staying far away, out where the wilderness is. That's the escape he's wishing for.
The temple is a good guess, but that's not where his wish lands. He says, "In the wilderness I would remain." He wants distance from the storm, and the wilderness is how he says it.

David says, "I would hurry to my shelter, far from this raging tempest." Hurry is the word he picks, and it tells you how badly he wants a safe place. He calls what he's in a raging tempest. I think a shelter sounds mighty good in the middle of that.

The city is the problem, not the escape. David says he sees "…violence and strife in the city." What he wants is to hurry "…to my shelter, far from this raging tempest." Running toward the trouble is not in his wish.
David doesn't mention any court in this wish. He says, "I would hurry to my shelter, far from this raging tempest." His dream is a quiet place away from all of it. No meetings and no crowds.

explanations.answer: He sees violence and strife in the city
explanations.explanation: David gives his reason right in the verse: "…for I see violence and strife in the city." He's asking the Lord to confuse and confound their speech. The reason is what he sees happening around him. He doesn't hold it in, he brings it to God.

explanations.answer: They have been worshiping other gods
explanations.explanation: The psalm never says that about them here. David asks the Lord to confuse their speech "…for I see violence and strife in the city." Violence and strife are what he's looking at, so that's what he prays about. I think when the city looks like that, other gods aren't the first thing on his mind.

explanations.answer: They refused to pay the temple tax
explanations.explanation: No tax in sight. David gives his reason plainly: "…for I see violence and strife in the city." It's what he sees that sends him to prayer.
David says the opposite. He says that "…malice and trouble lie within." the walls. He also says "oppression and deceit never leave the streets." So the streets are where the trouble lives.

Right, the inside is no safer. David says, "Day and night they encircle the walls, while malice and trouble lie within." He adds, "Destruction is within…" and "oppression and deceit never leave the streets." So the trouble circles the walls, and it's inside too.

David says, "But it is you, a man like myself, my companion and close friend." The word hits harder because of who it is. Right before this he says an enemy's insults he could endure. This one comes from someone close.
David never calls him a brother. He says, "But it is you, a man like myself, my companion and close friend." The psalm says friend, and that word is why this one stings.
David doesn't make this man a servant. He says, "But it is you, a man like myself, my companion and close friend." He's an equal, a man like David, and that's the whole sting.

David says, "We shared sweet fellowship together; we walked with the crowd into the house of God." So they walked into the house of God together, with the crowd. That's a lot of shared road behind them. I think that's why the turn hurts so much.

It's true, actually. David says, "We shared sweet fellowship together; we walked with the crowd into the house of God." They went in together with the crowd. So this wasn't a stranger, it was someone he had walked beside.

David says, "But I call to God, and the LORD saves me." Notice the "But." Everything before it is hurt and fear, and then he turns toward God. He doesn't pretend it's not hard, he just takes it to the right place.
Leaving was his wish, with those dove wings. But what he actually says is, "But I call to God, and the LORD saves me." The dream was running away, and the real answer is a prayer.

The psalm never says David gathers anybody. He says, "But I call to God, and the LORD saves me." Nobody gets a roll call, he just calls on God. I bet that's one phone call that never goes to voicemail, but that's me talking, not the psalm.
David says the opposite. He says, "Morning, noon, and night, I cry out in distress, and He hears my voice." The verse says God hears him. Nothing in it says God gets tired of hearing him.

Right. David says, "Morning, noon, and night, I cry out in distress, and He hears my voice." He cries out morning, noon and night, and he says God hears his voice. Nothing there says God gets tired of it.

explanations.answer: They don't change and have no fear of God
explanations.explanation: David says it's "…because they do not change and they have no fear of God." He names God as "…the One enthroned for the ages…" the One who hears. The reason is about who they are and how they treat God. Nothing else is added.

explanations.answer: They don't keep the Sabbath day holy
explanations.explanation: The Sabbath isn't mentioned here. David gives the reason himself: "…because they do not change and they have no fear of God." He says it right after calling God the One "…enthroned for the ages…"

explanations.answer: They don't bring offerings to the temple
explanations.explanation: Offerings aren't mentioned in this part of the psalm. David says it's "…because they do not change and they have no fear of God." That's the reason the text gives, and it's about who they are, not what they skipped bringing. I'd have loved to hand out a checklist, but the psalm doesn't have one.

explanations.answer: His words sound kind but he means harm
explanations.explanation: David says, "His speech is smooth as butter, but war is in his heart." Then he says the words are "…softer than oil, yet they are swords unsheathed." So the voice sounds gentle while the heart means battle. Butter and oil, and still the blade is out.

explanations.answer: His words sound harsh but he means well
explanations.explanation: That's flipped. David says, "His speech is smooth as butter, but war is in his heart." The words are the soft part, and the heart is where the war is. Smooth on the outside, swords on the inside.

explanations.answer: His words are true but he rarely speaks
explanations.explanation: David doesn't say a word about how often this man talks. He says, "His speech is smooth as butter, but war is in his heart." The point is the gap between the soft sound and the heart behind it.

David says, "Cast your burden upon the LORD and He will sustain you…" Cast it means throw it, not set it down gently and keep a hand on it. Then he adds the promise that God will sustain you. Peter, one of Jesus' apostles, says something close: "Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you." (1 Peter 5:7)
David doesn't send the burden to any king. He says, "Cast your burden upon the LORD and He will sustain you…" The LORD is the one who sustains. A throne in Jerusalem isn't the answer here.

The priests aren't named in this verse. David says, "Cast your burden upon the LORD and He will sustain you…" The burden goes straight to the LORD, with no middleman. Think of it like a heavy box of cookies, and he's saying hand it to the One who can hold it.
David says the opposite. He says, "He will never let the righteous be shaken." Never is a strong word. He puts it right after "Cast your burden upon the LORD and He will sustain you…"
Right. David says, "He will never let the righteous be shaken." Never, not now and then. That promise comes right after he says the LORD will sustain you.

David closes with "But I will trust in You." After the pounding heart, the violent city, and the friend who turned, he lands on trust. He doesn't say the trouble was small. I think that's what makes the last line so strong.
Singing is a fine thing, but that's not his last word here. David ends with "But I will trust in You." After everything he just described, trust is where he lands.
David doesn't end with bragging. He ends with "But I will trust in You." After the fear and the betrayal, he puts his weight on God, not on himself.
